title: Through a microscope: the tiny world on a glass slide
description: A single drop of pond water, a flake of onion skin, the edge of a feather — under a microscope the most ordinary things turn into landscapes. What the lenses are really doing, and what to look at first.

body.heading: Two lenses are better than one
paragraphs: A school microscope does not magnify once but twice. The objective lens, close to the slide, makes a first enlarged image; the eyepiece lens magnifies that image again. Multiply the two numbers printed on the lenses — often 10 times 10 — and you get the total: a hundred times bigger than life.

Light matters as much as lenses. Most slides are lit from below, which is why specimens must be thin enough for light to pass through. A thick, dark object under a microscope is just a black shape; a thin slice of the same thing is a city of cells.

body.heading: First things to look at
paragraphs: Start with onion skin: peel the papery inner layer, lay it flat in a drop of water, and you will see neat brick-like rows — plant cells, with their walls in tidy lines. It is the view that first showed generations of students that living things are built, not just grown.

Then try a drop of pond water and be patient. Among the drifting specks you may spot single-celled creatures rowing themselves along with tiny hairs, changing shape, utterly unaware they are being watched. Early microscopes in the 1600s revealed this whole invisible world for the first time — bacteria included — and changed medicine forever.

body.heading: Focus like a scientist
paragraphs: Always start on the lowest power and focus there first; hunting on high power is how slides get cracked by a lens driven down into them. Move the slide slowly — at a hundred times magnification, a millimetre is a journey.
Draw what you see, with the magnification written beside it. A drawing forces your eye to actually look, and it is still what biologists do, three and a half centuries after the first microscopes.

takeaway: A microscope stacks two magnifications and needs thin, backlit specimens — start with onion skin cells, then go hunting in a drop of pond water.
